title: The checks I run on every backtest an LLM writes for me, after my AI agents "beat" a simulated market for the wrong reasons
author: Individual-Quote-958
selftext:
Back in April I built a sandbox where a few AI agents traded against each other in a simulated market. A lot of them "won". When I went through why, it was mostly two things: lookahead bias that had crept into the sim, and the models already knowing those prices from their training data. They weren't predicting anything, they were remembering.

Since then I've been pretty paranoid about LLM-written backtests. These are the checks I run now, roughly in order of how often they catch something.

1. Is the signal using the bar it trades on?

This is the most common bug I see in LLM backtest code:

```
df["pos"] = (df["close"] > df["close"].rolling(20).mean()).astype(int)
df["strat"] = df["pos"] * df["close"].pct_change()
```

The position is decided on today's close and earns today's return. You can't trade that. Shift it: df["pos"].shift(1). Better still, set things up so a decision on a bar can only use that bar's open, and fills happen on the next bar. If the results fall apart after the shift, you found it.

2. Anything computed on the full series.

Z-scores using the whole-sample mean and std, scalers fit on all the data, "normalize by max price", regime labels assigned with hindsight. These leak the future in a way that's harder to spot than a missing shift. Everything should be rolling or expanding.

3. The model knows what happened.

If you ask for "a strategy for NVDA", the model knows how NVDA did. It will happily build something that's long in exactly the right years without meaning to. Test the idea on tickers and periods it wasn't inspired by, and weight data after the model's training cutoff more heavily. Forward paper trading is the one test it can't have memorized.

4. Parameter sweeps reported as results.

If the LLM tried 30 combinations and showed you the best one, that's a selection result, not a strategy. Do walk-forward: pick parameters on an in-sample window, then run them untouched out of sample. If out-of-sample falls apart, call it overfit and move on.

5. Fills and costs.

Filling at the same bar's close, zero fees, zero slippage, no borrow cost on shorts. Add realistic costs before you get attached to anything, especially higher-turnover stuff.

6. A dumb baseline.

Random entries with the same holding period and exposure. If the strategy doesn't clearly beat that, the "edge" is probably just market exposure.

The mindset change that helped me most: the default answer for a new idea should be "not good enough yet", and the backtest's job is to try to prove that, not confirm the idea.

Disclosure: I'm the founder of Polarline, and the sandbox mess above is why I built Scout. It's a terminal agent that turns a plain-English idea into Python, then runs walk-forward, Monte Carlo and lookahead checks on it and defaults to a research_only verdict. Happy to just talk about the checks though. What have you caught that isn't on this list?

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: I’d add a point-in-time data audit. Even after fixing the rolling-20 signal with \`shift(1)\`, an LLM can silently test today’s constituents, adjusted prices, or revised fundamentals across the past. That creates survivorship and revision leakage without any obvious same-bar bug. For the NVDA-style cross-ticker test, save the universe membership, corporate-action treatment, and source vintage available on each date, then rerun with delisted names included. Forward paper trading avoids memorized prices, but it will not reveal that the historical dataset itself knew the future.

replies.author: Individual-Quote-958
replies.body: Good one, and sneakier than the shift bug because the code looks totally clean. Saving the universe and data vintage per date is a nice way to make it checkable instead of just trusting the vendor. Adding it to my list.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: memorization is the nasty one, since the shift test can't see it. code can pass every leak check and still be the model reciting 2023. the shift bug is why I built Quantradin the way it is: decide on one bar, fill on the next, options at the bid and ask. quantradin.com. do you also rerun with the ticker name hidden?

replies.author: Individual-Quote-958
replies.body: Sometimes, yeah. Hiding the ticker and shifting the dates helps a bit, but the model can still recognize the shape of famous moves like 2020 or 2022. I trust held-out tickers and data after the training cutoff more.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: post-cutoff data is what I'd trust most too. held-out tickers help less than people think, because in 2020 and 2022 nearly everything moved together, so a model that remembers SPY roughly remembers the whole tape that year.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good list, and the shift(1) example is exactly the bug I see most. One that isn't on it: survivorship in the data itself. A backtest on today's index members, or on tickers that still exist, leaves out every company that was delisted or taken over, which flatters almost any long strategy and no amount of walk-forward testing catches it. A related one is timestamps on fundamentals and events, where a number that was revised or published later gets attached to the date it describes, so the model quietly trades on information from the future. Cymetica's EventTrader is one example of a dataset built around when each piece of information actually became known.

replies.author: Individual-Quote-958
replies.body: Yeah, survivorship is a big one I left off. Free data is the worst for it since the delisted names just aren't there, so a dip-buying test on today's index quietly only buys the ones that recovered. Release date vs period date on fundamentals is an easy one to miss too.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Right, and the dip-buying example is the cleanest way to explain it: the test can only ever buy the dips that recovered. A quick sanity check for any free dataset is to look up a few companies you know were delisted or bought out (for example from the 2008 or 2022 bear markets) and see if they exist in the data at all. If they don't, every long test on it is flattered. Thanks for adding the release date point too.

comments.author: Maleficent-Success-6
comments.body:
Good checklist. One additional test I'd automate is future-data perturbation.

Freeze the dataset at timestamp T and run the strategy.

Then modify or append data strictly after T and run it again.

Every signal, position size and trading decision at or before T should remain identical.

If changing future observations changes past decisions, something is leaking information backward, even if the obvious shift(1) errors have been fixed.

I'd make this an automated regression test rather than relying entirely on code review.

Another useful check is replay consistency: feed the same recorded market events into the strategy engine and compare the resulting decisions and order requests.

That won't prove the simulated fills match real execution, but it helps separate strategy inconsistencies from execution-model differences.

I'd also preserve the full experiment history when an LLM proposes multiple variations. The unsuccessful versions matter because they consume research freedom too.

Have you tried adding these kinds of invariance tests to your automated validation pipeline?

comments.author: investigatormaker
comments.body:
Two I'd add. Survivorship: if the LLM builds the universe from today's S&P 500 list, every backtest quietly drops the companies that went bust or got delisted, and the code itself looks clean. And point-in-time data: fundamentals or earnings joined on the period-end date instead of the release date leak weeks of hindsight, the same family as your full-series z-scores. If Scout doesn't flag a current-constituents universe already, that check would catch the first before anyone gets excited about a Sharpe ratio.

comments.author: Tasty-Mammoth5321
comments.body:
The truncation test caught more for me than any of the manual checks. You run the same signal code once on the full series and once on data cut off at time t, then compare what it says at t. If the two differ, something is reading the future. I did this on nine detectors and rules in my own event testing, all written with LLM help, and seven of them leaked, mostly by picking up candles or messages stamped after the decision time.

Two more that were not on your list. Batched events: I had a sub strategy with 10 winners out of 12 that turned out to be nine entries in the same second on one red day, so really four to six independent observations. Clustering by week took one t of 4.7 down to 2.5. And the sweep problem does not stay inside a single run. After a few dozen separate tests over several weeks, the best hour of the day looked significant at a t of about 2.6, so I raised my bar to 3 for everything.

Small but nasty: timestamps. One news source stamps posts in UTC+8, and assuming local time shifts every event by an hour.
